title: One leader, many followers: sync, async and failover
goal: By the end you can explain why a database keeps copies on other machines, how one leader orders every write into a log that followers replay, what asynchronous, synchronous and semi-synchronous replication each promise when the client hears OK, how a new follower starts from a snapshot and a log position, and what a failover can lose.

warmup.q: Your payments database has a leader and two followers. So that no acknowledged payment can ever be lost, you make the leader wait for both followers before it says OK. One follower's VM is paused for 40 seconds by a host migration. What happens to payments during those 40 seconds?
options: The leader skips the paused follower and waits only for the other one
Every commit waits until the paused follower answers again, so payments stop for up to 40 seconds
Commits fail fast with an error, so the service can retry somewhere else
The cluster removes the paused follower automatically after a few seconds
warmup.why: If the rule is "wait for both", a commit can't be acknowledged until both have confirmed, and a paused follower confirms nothing. Every payment waits, and the slowest follower sets everyone's latency. That is why real systems wait for one follower, or for a majority, and why some quietly drop the rule when a follower stops answering (MySQL's semi-sync falls back to asynchronous after a timeout). Removing a follower automatically is something a failover tool might do, but the replication protocol itself just waits.

sections.h: Copies on other machines, and one machine that orders the writes
sections.body:
One PostgreSQL server holds the ledger for a card processor, and that one server causes three problems. When its disk dies, every payment since the last backup is gone, and nothing takes a write until someone builds a new machine. A merchant dashboard in Singapore that reads from it in Virginia pays a round trip of over 200 ms on every query. And when the month-end reports start, they fight the card authorizations for the same CPU and disk.

All three have the same answer: keep copies of the data on more machines. A copy in another zone survives the disk or the building. A copy near the merchant answers reads locally. Five copies can serve five times the reads. A copy that holds all of the data and keeps up with every change is a **replica**. This track assumes every replica holds the whole database; the Partitioning track drops that assumption.

Copying data that never changes is easy: copy it once. The hard part is every change after that.

Start with the simplest version: the application sends every write to every copy. Two clients update payment pay-77 at almost the same moment. Client A sends `captured` at 0 ms, client B sends `refunded` at 1 ms. Copy X is 2 ms from A and 9 ms from B, so it applies captured, then refunded. Copy Y is 8 ms from A and 3 ms from B, so it applies refunded, then captured. Each copy did exactly what it was told, and now one says the money went back and the other says it didn't. Nothing will repair this later, because neither copy knows it is wrong.

The copies disagree because nobody decided the order. So let one node decide. That node is the **leader** (PostgreSQL calls it the primary, MySQL the source). Every write goes to the leader. The leader applies it, appends it to its log and gives it the next position: 1, 2, 3. The other nodes are **followers** (standbys, replicas, secondaries). Each one reads the leader's log and applies the entries strictly in position order. Two copies that start from the same data and apply the same entries in the same order end up with the same data. Writes go only to the leader; reads can go to any copy.

That is single-leader replication, and its picture runs through the whole lesson: one ordered log, and each follower at some position in it. A follower's position is the one number that says how up to date it is. When may the leader say OK, how does a new follower start, what does a failover lose: each is a question about positions.

Most databases you use work this way, under different names:

| System | Leader | Followers | The log | A position looks like |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| PostgreSQL | primary | standbys | write-ahead log (WAL) | an LSN, `0/50DF770` |
| MySQL | source | replicas | binary log | file and offset, or a GTID |
| MongoDB | primary | secondaries | oplog | a timestamp |
| Redis | master | replicas | replication stream | a byte offset |
| Kafka | partition leader | followers | the partition | an offset |

Redis's version is in the Caching track's lesson on persistence and replication. Kafka's comes in the Messaging track's lesson on the cluster. Oracle Data Guard, which you may run at work, is the same shape.

try.title: Two writers and no leader, then one leader
steps: Run the demo from the `labs` folder. It plays the pay-77 story above on simulated time, first with each client writing to both copies, then with copy X as the leader and copy Y following its log.

Predict before you run it again with `-Pargs='3 9'`, which makes client B 3 ms from copy X and 9 ms from copy Y: do the two copies agree without a leader this time? Does that make the leaderless version safe?
try.expect:
Without a leader the copies end up disagreeing; with one they agree:

```text
No leader: each client writes to both copies
    2 ms  copy X applies captured  (from client A)
    4 ms  copy Y applies refunded  (from client B)
    8 ms  copy Y applies captured  (from client A)
   10 ms  copy X applies refunded  (from client B)
  copy X says pay-77 is refunded, copy Y says captured
One leader (copy X): it puts the updates in its log, the follower (copy Y) applies the log in order
    2 ms  leader X logs position 1: captured  (from client A)
    8 ms  follower Y applies position 1: captured
   10 ms  leader X logs position 2: refunded  (from client B)
   16 ms  follower Y applies position 2: refunded
  leader X says pay-77 is refunded, follower Y says refunded
```

With `-Pargs='3 9'` both copies happen to get the updates in the same order and agree. That is luck: the next pair of writes can arrive the other way round. With a leader, the order is a fact in the log that every follower reads.

sections.h: When does the leader say OK? Synchronous, asynchronous and semi-synchronous
sections.body:
A client sends a payment to the leader. The leader writes it to its own log on its own disk and ships the entry to the followers. At some moment it tells the client OK. Which moment you choose decides what a dying leader can take with it.

The fastest choice is **asynchronous**: say OK as soon as the entry is on the leader's disk, and ship it in the background. The client never waits for the network. A follower is usually a few milliseconds behind, but nothing bounds that. A follower replaying one huge transaction, catching up after a restart or behind a congested link can be seconds or minutes behind. If the leader dies then, the payments in between exist on no surviving machine, although their clients heard OK.

The safest-looking choice is fully synchronous: say OK only when every follower has confirmed the entry. Then any follower can take over and lose nothing. It breaks at once. Each commit waits for the slowest follower's round trip, and a follower that is paused, rebooting or cut off stops every write until it returns or someone removes it. That is the warm-up: with both followers synchronous, one paused VM stops payments for 40 seconds.

Most systems choose the middle: wait for some followers, not all. Wait for any one follower, and every acknowledged write is on at least two machines; if that follower dies, another can take its place. This is usually called **semi-synchronous** replication. Wait for a majority (two of three, three of five) and you have a quorum, which the Consistency and consensus track turns into Raft.

The lab's simulator puts numbers on it. One leader, f1 20 ms away and f2 50 ms away (one way), a payment every 4 ms, and the leader dies at 1,001 ms:

| The leader says OK when | Each commit waits | OKs in the first second | Lost at failover |
|---|---|---|---|
| its own disk has it | 0 ms | 250 | 4 |
| one follower has it | 40 ms | 241 | 0 |
| both followers have it | 100 ms | 226 | 0 |

Real round trips are about 1 ms between zones of one cloud region and about 70 ms between regions. The shape stays the same.

"A follower has it" can mean four things, and the figure shows them. The entry can be in the follower's memory, handed to its operating system, flushed to its disk, or applied so queries there can see it. PostgreSQL lets each transaction choose with `synchronous_commit` (lesson 4 runs it on a real primary). A MySQL semi-synchronous replica confirms once the events are written and flushed to its relay log, before it has executed them.

Read the fine print on what happens when no follower answers. MySQL's source waits up to `rpl_semi_sync_source_timeout`, 10 seconds by default. Then, in the manual's words, it "reverts to asynchronous replication", and it goes back to semi-sync only when a replica catches up. No error reaches any client. One commit takes 10 seconds, every later commit is fast, and the database is now asynchronous; the only sign is the status variable `Rpl_semi_sync_source_status` dropping to 0. PostgreSQL does the opposite and keeps every commit waiting. Kafka has its own version: `acks=all` waits for the in-sync replicas, a set that can shrink to the leader alone (the Messaging track covers `min.insync.replicas`).

try.title: Commit latency and lost writes, per mode
steps: Run the demo from the `labs` folder. It runs the lesson's cluster four times in simulated time, once per mode, crashes the leader at 1,001 ms and promotes the most up-to-date follower. Then it runs semi-sync again with both followers stalled 600 and 700 ms away.
Predict the last row before you look: the followers are slower than the 500 ms timeout. How long does a commit wait, and what does the failover lose?
Run it with `-Pargs='2 70'`: f1 in the same zone, f2 in another region. Which modes got cheaper, and why didn't waiting for both followers?
try.expect:
The default run:

```text
leader -> f1 20 ms, leader -> f2 50 ms (one way); a payment every 4 ms; the leader dies at 1,001 ms

mode                        commit p50 commit max  said OK  new leader  lost
async                             0 ms       0 ms      250   f1 at 246     4
sync, 1 of 2 followers           40 ms      40 ms      241   f1 at 246     0
sync, both followers            100 ms     100 ms      226   f1 at 246     0
semi-sync, timeout 500 ms        40 ms      40 ms      241   f1 at 246     0

The same semi-sync leader, with both followers stalled (600 and 700 ms away):
semi-sync, timeout 500 ms         4 ms     500 ms      250   f1 at 101   149
  semi-sync switched itself off at 500 ms and stayed off: every later commit returned at once
```

A healthy semi-sync leader behaves like "wait for one". A stalled one makes the first payment wait the full 500 ms, then switches to asynchronous without telling anyone, and the failover loses 149 payments that were acknowledged under a setting called semi-synchronous. With `-Pargs='2 70'`, waiting for one follower costs 4 ms (f1's round trip) and nothing is lost even asynchronously, because f1 had every entry 2 ms after it was written. Waiting for both now costs 140 ms: you pay for the farthest follower on every commit.

sections.h: A new follower starts from a snapshot and a log position
sections.body:
Followers die and get replaced, and you add more as reads grow. A new follower needs the leader's data, and the leader can't stop for it. Copy the data files while payments keep arriving, and some pages in the copy are from 10:00 and others from 10:20: a state the database was never in. Lock the leader while you copy 2 TB, and payments stop for hours.

The way out is to remember exactly where the copy was taken:

1. Take a consistent snapshot of the leader's data without stopping writes, and note the log position it reflects.
2. Copy the snapshot to the new machine and load it.
3. Ask the leader for every entry after that position, and apply them in order.
4. Once caught up, keep streaming like any other follower.

The position is what makes it work. Start replay one entry too late, and the follower silently lacks a write forever. Start too early, and it applies writes it already has; if an entry says "add 30 cents to the fee", the fee is charged twice (lesson 2 shows which kinds of log survive that).

Every database ships this recipe. PostgreSQL's `pg_basebackup` copies a running server's data directory plus the WAL written during the copy, and the standby streams on from where the copy ended (lesson 4 builds one). MySQL's clone plugin, or a dump that records the binary log coordinates or GTID set it was taken at, does the same. A new MongoDB secondary runs an initial sync: it copies every collection, then applies the oplog entries written since the copy began. A new Redis replica gets a full resync: a snapshot (an RDB file) plus the writes that arrived while it was made.

The same position lets a follower that was away for a while catch up cheaply. It reconnects and says "send me everything after 4,812". The leader can do that only if it still has those entries, and that is a real trade-off. Keep the log until every follower has it, and one follower that is down for a week fills the leader's disk; PostgreSQL's replication slots work this way, which is why PostgreSQL 18 added `idle_replication_slot_timeout` (lesson 4). Keep only a fixed amount, and a follower that falls further behind must be rebuilt from a new snapshot. MongoDB's oplog window and Redis's replication backlog work this way: Redis resumes with `PSYNC <replication id> <offset>`, a partial resync if the backlog still covers the gap and a full one otherwise.

Rebuilding a big follower is slower than the arithmetic says. In GitHub's 2018 outage (next section), restoring several terabytes from backup took hours, and catch-up afterwards kept slowing down, so the time-to-recover estimates were wrong. Plan for hours, and keep a spare follower so you rarely need to rebuild in a hurry.

try.title: Watch a follower fall behind and catch up
steps: Run the demo from the `labs` folder. A payment is written every 10 ms, and the link to f1 is cut from 200 to 500 ms.
Before you read the output: when the link comes back, what tells f1 that it missed something, and what does it ask the leader for?
Run it again with `-Pargs='90'`, so the leader keeps its last 90 entries instead of 20. Does f1 still need a snapshot?
try.expect:
```text
  100 ms  leader at  11, f1 at  10
  199 ms  leader at  20, f1 at  20   (the link to f1 is cut at 200 ms)
  300 ms  leader at  31, f1 at  20
  499 ms  leader at  50, f1 at  20   (the link comes back at 500 ms)
  516 ms  leader at  52, f1 at  20   (entry 52 arrived at 515: f1 sees a gap after 20 and asks for everything after 20)
  526 ms  leader at  53, f1 at  53   (entries 21 to 53 arrived at 525)
 1000 ms  leader at 100, f1 at 100

Again, but the leader keeps only its last 20 log entries when f1 comes back:
  f1 asks for entries after 20: leader: entries after 20 are gone (oldest kept: 81); rebuild from a snapshot
  f1 restored from a snapshot at position 100; rows match the leader: true
```

The gap is the signal: entry 52 arrives when f1 is at 20, so it refuses to apply it and asks for everything after 20. One round trip later it is caught up. When the leader has thrown those entries away, the position alone is no use, and f1 has to start again from a snapshot. With 90 entries kept, entries 21 to 100 are all there, and f1 applies 80 entries instead.

sections.h: Failover: notice, choose, redirect, and what each step breaks
sections.body:
Sooner or later the leader dies. The followers can still serve reads, but nothing accepts a write until one of them becomes the leader. That is **failover**, and it has three steps. The stepper walks through them with the lab's numbers.

Notice. Nothing tells a follower that the leader is dead; it only notices that the leader went quiet. So every system uses a timeout. MongoDB's members call an election after `electionTimeoutMillis`, 10 seconds by default, and the manual says the median time to elect a new primary should not typically exceed 12 seconds. Patroni, the usual failover manager for PostgreSQL, uses a 30-second leader lease. Too long a timeout, and payments fail for all of it. Too short, and a leader that is only slow (a long garbage-collection pause, a load spike) gets replaced, and its load lands on a node that was already struggling. This is why many teams fail over by hand. The Faults, time and truth track's lesson on detecting failure shows why no timeout is right for every case.

Choose. The follower with the highest position loses the least. With semi-synchronous replication, the follower the leader waited for has every acknowledged write. Agreeing on one choice while some nodes can't reach others is a consensus problem. Redis Cluster's replicas use a rule you can read in one line: wait 500 ms, plus up to 500 ms at random, plus one second per rank, where the most up-to-date replica has rank 0, so it usually asks for votes first.

Redirect. Writes must now go to the new leader: through a DNS name that moves, a proxy, or a driver that knows every host and asks which one leads. When the old leader comes back, it must rejoin as a follower.

Each step can hurt you. Under asynchronous replication the new leader lacks the old leader's last entries. When the old leader returns, its extra writes clash with the new history, and the usual fix throws them away (MongoDB writes them to a rollback directory; PostgreSQL's `pg_rewind` discards them). Clients were told OK for payments that no longer exist.

Ids get reused too. The new leader's auto-increment counter starts after the highest id it holds, so it hands out the lost rows' ids again. If those ids are also keys in a cache, a search index or another service, they now point at different rows. GitHub hit this in September 2012: an out-of-date MySQL server was promoted, ids generated in MySQL no longer matched what Redis held, and for seven minutes 16 private repositories were visible to people outside their teams.

And there can be two leaders. If the old one was only cut off, it may still take writes from clients that can reach it. Two nodes now accept writes and issue the same ids: **split brain**. The fix is fencing: make sure the old leader can't write (power it off, revoke its lease, cut it off) before the new one starts. Lesson 4 shows split brain on two real PostgreSQL servers, and the Faults track's lesson on leases and fencing tokens shows how to fence properly.

GitHub's outage of 21 October 2018 had all of this at once. At 22:52 UTC, work on optical equipment cut the link between its US East Coast hub and its main East Coast data center for 43 seconds. Orchestrator, its MySQL failover tool (which agrees through Raft), formed a majority from nodes in US West and an East Coast public cloud, and promoted primaries in the West. Applications wrote there for nearly 40 minutes, while the East primaries still held several seconds of writes the West never got. Each side now had writes the other lacked, and East Coast applications couldn't live with a cross-country round trip on most database calls. GitHub chose its data over its uptime: the site was degraded for 24 hours and 11 minutes while it restored and reconciled (one of the busiest clusters had 954 writes in the affected window). Afterwards it stopped Orchestrator from promoting primaries across regions.

stepper.intro: One leader, two followers, a payment every 4 ms. Click Next to crash the leader.

frames.say: The leader has written 250 payments and told every client OK. Replication is asynchronous, so the followers are where the network has got them: f1, 20 ms away, has applied up to position 246; f2, 50 ms away, up to 238. These are the lab's numbers: a payment every 4 ms, a crash at 1,001 ms.

frames.say: The leader's host dies. Entries 247 to 250 were on their way to f1 and are lost with the leader's network. Their clients already heard OK. Nothing is wrong yet from the followers' point of view: they simply hear nothing.

frames.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 300" role="img" aria-label="A leader and two followers during an asynchronous failover"><defs><marker id="arr" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M0 0L10 5L0 10z" class="ln"/></marker></defs><text class="t-s t-m" x="20" y="26" text-anchor="start">1,001 ms + timeout</text><rect class="box-bad" x="40" y="92" width="190" height="86" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="135.0" y="122.0" text-anchor="middle">leader: crashed</text><text class="t-s" x="135.0" y="140.0" text-anchor="middle">250 on its disk</text><text class="t-s" x="135.0" y="158.0" text-anchor="middle">unreachable</text><rect class="box-a" x="410" y="36" width="200" height="76" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="510.0" y="61.0" text-anchor="middle">f1</text><text class="t-s" x="510.0" y="79.0" text-anchor="middle">position 246</text><text class="t-s" x="510.0" y="97.0" text-anchor="middle">no heartbeat: dead?</text><rect class="box-a" x="410" y="160" width="200" height="76" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="510.0" y="185.0" text-anchor="middle">f2</text><text class="t-s" x="510.0" y="203.0" text-anchor="middle">position 238</text><text class="t-s" x="510.0" y="221.0" text-anchor="middle">no heartbeat: dead?</text><line class="ln-d" x1="230" y1="120" x2="408" y2="78" marker-end="url(#arr)"/><line class="ln-d" x1="230" y1="150" x2="408" y2="192" marker-end="url(#arr)"/><rect class="box" x="40" y="250" width="570" height="40" rx="8"/><text class="t-s" x="325.0" y="275.0" text-anchor="middle">every write fails until a follower takes over</text></svg>
frames.say: **Notice.** The followers can't tell a dead leader from a slow one or a broken link. They wait for a timeout: 10 seconds by default in MongoDB, a 30-second lease with Patroni for PostgreSQL. Every write fails for that long.

frames.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 300" role="img" aria-label="A leader and two followers during an asynchronous failover"><defs><marker id="arr" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M0 0L10 5L0 10z" class="ln"/></marker></defs><text class="t-s t-m" x="20" y="26" text-anchor="start">choose</text><rect class="box-bad" x="40" y="92" width="190" height="86" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="135.0" y="122.0" text-anchor="middle">leader: crashed</text><text class="t-s" x="135.0" y="140.0" text-anchor="middle">250 on its disk</text><text class="t-s" x="135.0" y="158.0" text-anchor="middle">unreachable</text><rect class="box-a" x="410" y="36" width="200" height="76" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="510.0" y="61.0" text-anchor="middle">f1: new leader</text><text class="t-s" x="510.0" y="79.0" text-anchor="middle">position 246</text><text class="t-s" x="510.0" y="97.0" text-anchor="middle">next id: 247</text><rect class="box" x="410" y="160" width="200" height="76" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="510.0" y="185.0" text-anchor="middle">f2</text><text class="t-s" x="510.0" y="203.0" text-anchor="middle">position 238</text><text class="t-s" x="510.0" y="221.0" text-anchor="middle">follows f1</text><line class="ln-d" x1="230" y1="120" x2="408" y2="78" marker-end="url(#arr)"/><line class="ln-d" x1="230" y1="150" x2="408" y2="192" marker-end="url(#arr)"/><line class="ln-a" x1="510" y1="112" x2="510" y2="158" marker-end="url(#arr)"/><rect class="box" x="40" y="250" width="570" height="40" rx="8"/><text class="t-s" x="325.0" y="275.0" text-anchor="middle">f2 catches up from f1: entries 239 to 246</text></svg>
frames.say: **Choose.** The follower with the highest position loses the least, so f1 is promoted. f2 starts following f1 and fetches entries 239 to 246 from it. f1's auto-increment counter restarts after the highest id it holds: 247.

frames.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 300" role="img" aria-label="A leader and two followers during an asynchronous failover"><defs><marker id="arr" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M0 0L10 5L0 10z" class="ln"/></marker></defs><text class="t-s t-m" x="20" y="26" text-anchor="start">redirect</text><rect class="box-bad" x="40" y="92" width="190" height="86" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="135.0" y="122.0" text-anchor="middle">leader: crashed</text><text class="t-s" x="135.0" y="140.0" text-anchor="middle">250 on its disk</text><text class="t-s" x="135.0" y="158.0" text-anchor="middle">unreachable</text><rect class="box" x="410" y="36" width="200" height="76" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="510.0" y="61.0" text-anchor="middle">f1: leader</text><text class="t-s" x="510.0" y="79.0" text-anchor="middle">position 250</text><text class="t-s" x="510.0" y="97.0" text-anchor="middle">refund-1 got id 247</text><rect class="box" x="410" y="160" width="200" height="76" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="510.0" y="185.0" text-anchor="middle">f2</text><text class="t-s" x="510.0" y="203.0" text-anchor="middle">position 250</text><text class="t-s" x="510.0" y="221.0" text-anchor="middle">follows f1</text><line class="ln-a" x1="510" y1="112" x2="510" y2="158" marker-end="url(#arr)"/><rect class="box-bad" x="40" y="250" width="570" height="40" rx="8"/><text class="t-s" x="325.0" y="275.0" text-anchor="middle">the cache still says id 247 is pay-247; the database says refund-1</text></svg>
frames.say: **Redirect.** Clients find f1 (a moved DNS name, a proxy, or a driver that asks each host) and carry on. The next four rows get ids 247 to 250, the ids of the lost payments. A cache filled before the crash still maps those ids to the old payments. This is GitHub's 2012 failure, in miniature.

frames.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 300" role="img" aria-label="A leader and two followers during an asynchronous failover"><defs><marker id="arr" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M0 0L10 5L0 10z" class="ln"/></marker></defs><text class="t-s t-m" x="20" y="26" text-anchor="start">later</text><rect class="box-bad" x="40" y="92" width="190" height="86" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="135.0" y="122.0" text-anchor="middle">old leader: back</text><text class="t-s" x="135.0" y="140.0" text-anchor="middle">position 250</text><text class="t-s" x="135.0" y="158.0" text-anchor="middle">thinks it leads</text><rect class="box" x="410" y="36" width="200" height="76" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="510.0" y="61.0" text-anchor="middle">f1: leader</text><text class="t-s" x="510.0" y="79.0" text-anchor="middle">position 250</text><text class="t-s" x="510.0" y="97.0" text-anchor="middle">different 247 to 250</text><rect class="box" x="410" y="160" width="200" height="76" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="510.0" y="185.0" text-anchor="middle">f2</text><text class="t-s" x="510.0" y="203.0" text-anchor="middle">position 250</text><text class="t-s" x="510.0" y="221.0" text-anchor="middle">follows f1</text><line class="ln-a" x1="510" y1="112" x2="510" y2="158" marker-end="url(#arr)"/><rect class="box-bad" x="40" y="250" width="570" height="40" rx="8"/><text class="t-s" x="325.0" y="275.0" text-anchor="middle">two leaders accept writes: split brain</text></svg>
frames.say: The old leader's host reboots, or its network heals. It still has its own entries 247 to 250, and nothing has told it that it was replaced. Clients that still have its address can write to it. Two nodes accept writes and hand out the same ids: **split brain**.

frames.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 300" role="img" aria-label="A leader and two followers during an asynchronous failover"><defs><marker id="arr" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M0 0L10 5L0 10z" class="ln"/></marker></defs><text class="t-s t-m" x="20" y="26" text-anchor="start">fence and rejoin</text><rect class="box-dim" x="40" y="92" width="190" height="86" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="135.0" y="122.0" text-anchor="middle">old leader: fenced</text><text class="t-s" x="135.0" y="140.0" text-anchor="middle">rewound to 246</text><text class="t-s" x="135.0" y="158.0" text-anchor="middle">now follows f1</text><rect class="box-ok" x="410" y="36" width="200" height="76" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="510.0" y="61.0" text-anchor="middle">f1: leader</text><text class="t-s" x="510.0" y="79.0" text-anchor="middle">position 250</text><text class="t-s" x="510.0" y="97.0" text-anchor="middle">the only writer</text><rect class="box" x="410" y="160" width="200" height="76" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="510.0" y="185.0" text-anchor="middle">f2</text><text class="t-s" x="510.0" y="203.0" text-anchor="middle">position 250</text><text class="t-s" x="510.0" y="221.0" text-anchor="middle">follows f1</text><line class="ln-a" x1="510" y1="112" x2="510" y2="158" marker-end="url(#arr)"/><rect class="box-ok" x="40" y="250" width="570" height="40" rx="8"/><text class="t-s" x="325.0" y="275.0" text-anchor="middle">one leader again; 4 acknowledged payments are gone for good</text></svg>
frames.say: The fix is to fence the old leader before it can take writes (power it off, revoke its lease, cut it off) and bring it back only as a follower. It must throw away its own 247 to 250 first, as PostgreSQL's `pg_rewind` does. Those four payments were acknowledged and are lost: that is the price of asynchronous replication, paid at failover.

try.title: Lose four payments, then reuse their ids
steps: Run the demo from the `labs` folder. It is the stepper's cluster: after the crash it promotes the best follower and writes four refunds. A cache, filled with `id -> payment` whenever a client heard OK, stands in for GitHub's Redis.
Predict the ids the four refunds get. Then run it again with `-Pargs='sync'` (wait for one follower) and compare.
try.expect:
```text
mode: asynchronous
1,001 ms  the leader dies at position 250; clients have heard OK for 250 payments
          f1 has applied up to position 246
          f2 has applied up to position 238
          promote f1, the most up to date; its next id is 247
          acknowledged but not on f1: [pay-247, pay-248, pay-249, pay-250]

 1101 ms  the new leader stores refund-1 as id 247  <- the cache says id 247 is pay-247
 1102 ms  the new leader stores refund-2 as id 248  <- the cache says id 248 is pay-248
 1103 ms  the new leader stores refund-3 as id 249  <- the cache says id 249 is pay-249
 1104 ms  the new leader stores refund-4 as id 250  <- the cache says id 250 is pay-250
```

Four acknowledged payments are gone, and their ids now mean something else in the database than in the cache. With `sync`, clients have heard OK for 241 payments, nothing acknowledged is lost, and none of the reused ids (247 to 250) is in the cache, because no client was ever told those payments existed.

analogy: A bank branch with one head teller and two clerks who keep copies of the ledger. Only the head teller writes entries, and numbers each line; the clerks copy the lines in number order, so all three books agree. Asynchronous: the head teller tells the customer "done" as soon as the line is in her own book. Synchronous: she waits until a clerk calls back "copied line 812". If she collapses, the clerk with the highest line number takes over, and anything she wrote after his last line exists only in her book. If she recovers and keeps writing in her old book, the branch has two ledgers. The analogy breaks at the clock: a clerk who stops answering might be asleep or might be dead, and in a real system nobody can walk over and check.
in_your_world: Oracle Data Guard is single-leader replication: the primary ships redo to standbys, and its protection modes are the asynchronous, synchronous and "synchronous unless the standby is gone" choices from this lesson (lesson 4 maps them to PostgreSQL). Your Kafka topics are single-leader per partition, and `acks=all` is "wait for the followers in the ISR". The failover hazards land in your services as retries. During a failover a Quarkus endpoint can send a COMMIT and get a broken connection with no answer: the payment may be on the new leader, may have been lost, or may never have happened. Idempotency keys on every write make the retry safe either way. And if a service caches database ids in Redis or puts them in Kafka messages, an asynchronous failover can make those ids point at different rows: prefer keys you generate yourself (a UUIDv7, an idempotency key) for anything that leaves the database.
mistake: Turning on semi-synchronous replication and treating it as "no data loss". It is set once, it works on the day it is tested, and nobody looks at it again. Then a replica slows down for longer than `rpl_semi_sync_source_timeout`, the source silently switches to asynchronous, and the next failover loses acknowledged transactions. People make this mistake because the setting's name promises the property and nothing in the application ever errors. The fix: alert on `Rpl_semi_sync_source_status` = 0 (and on `Rpl_semi_sync_source_no_tx` rising), keep at least two semi-sync replicas so one slow one doesn't trip the timeout, and decide on purpose what the timeout should be: a short one keeps commits fast and accepts loss, a very long one keeps the guarantee and stops writes.

compare.title: Waiting for a follower: MySQL semi-sync and a PostgreSQL synchronous standby

a.label: MySQL 8.4
a.title: my.cnf on the source (plugin installed)
a.src:
rpl_semi_sync_source_enabled = ON
rpl_semi_sync_source_wait_for_replica_count = 1   # default
rpl_semi_sync_source_wait_point = AFTER_SYNC      # default: after the binlog
                                                  # sync, before the engine commit
rpl_semi_sync_source_timeout = 10000              # ms, default

# the replica acks once the events are flushed to its relay log
# timeout without an ack: the source reverts to asynchronous
# SHOW STATUS LIKE 'Rpl_semi_sync_source_status';  1 = waiting, 0 = async

b.label: PostgreSQL 18
b.title: postgresql.conf on the primary
b.src:
synchronous_standby_names = 'ANY 1 (s1, s2)'
synchronous_commit = on           # default: wait until a standby has
                                  # flushed the commit's WAL to disk
                                  # (remote_write, remote_apply: other points)

# no timeout: with no listed standby connected,
# every COMMIT waits until one comes back
# SELECT application_name, sync_state FROM pg_stat_replication;

compare.note: Both wait for one follower to have the commit on its disk before answering, so on a good day they promise the same thing. They differ when no follower answers. MySQL gives up after 10 seconds and becomes asynchronous, which keeps the service up and quietly drops the guarantee. PostgreSQL keeps every commit waiting, which keeps the guarantee and stops the service. Neither is wrong; each needs a second follower and an alert, and a failover tool such as Patroni can make PostgreSQL fall back on purpose.

worked.title: How much would a failover lose right now?

steps.say: Find the gap between the leader and its best follower, as a log position and as time. On PostgreSQL the primary reports both for every standby.
steps.code:
-- on the primary: bytes and time each standby is behind
SELECT application_name, sync_state,
       pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), flush_lsn) AS flush_behind_bytes,
       flush_lag, replay_lag
FROM pg_stat_replication;

steps.say: On MySQL, check that semi-sync is really on, not only enabled, and whether commits have gone through without an ack.
steps.code:
SHOW STATUS LIKE 'Rpl_semi_sync_source_status';   -- 1: waiting for replicas, 0: fell back to async
SHOW STATUS LIKE 'Rpl_semi_sync_source_no_tx';    -- commits that were never acknowledged by a replica

steps.say: On MongoDB, the shell prints how far each secondary is behind the primary.
steps.code: rs.printSecondaryReplicationInfo()   // each secondary's last applied oplog time and lag behind the primary

steps.say: Turn the gap into payments. If a flush lag of 250 ms is typical and the service commits 400 payments a second, an asynchronous failover at a typical moment loses about 100 acknowledged payments; at a bad moment (lag of 30 s during a catch-up) about 12,000.
steps.code:
lost ~= write rate x lag of the follower you would promote
       = 400 payments/s x 0.25 s = 100 payments   (typical)
       = 400 payments/s x 30 s  = 12,000 payments (during a catch-up)

steps.say: Decide per kind of write. Card authorizations go through a synchronous follower or carry idempotency keys the processor can reconcile; analytics events can stay asynchronous.

lab.title: A leader, two followers and a failover, in virtual time
steps: Run the tests from the `labs` folder; they need no Docker and finish in about a second, because `Sim` runs simulated time with no sleeping. All 22 fail. Read `Replication.kt` first: `Cluster` already ships entries over links with a delay, keeps messages on a link in order, drops messages to and from crashed nodes, and handles catch-up requests.

Exercise 1, `Node.apply`: apply entries in position order, skip ones you already have, stop at a gap. `CatchUpTest` builds a follower from a snapshot plus `entriesAfter(position)` and cuts a follower off for 300 ms.

Exercise 2, `Cluster.isAcknowledged`: when may the leader say OK? Asynchronous at once, synchronous once enough followers have confirmed, semi-synchronous after one confirmation or the timeout, whichever comes first, and after a timeout it switches itself off. `AckTest` checks the latencies the lesson's table shows.

Exercise 3, `Cluster.failover`: promote the live follower with the highest position, reset its id counter, and list the acknowledged writes it never had. `FailoverTest` counts them for each mode and reproduces the reused ids. The two property tests in `FailoverPropertyTest` then try 200 random delays and crash times each.
hints: `apply`: loop over the entries; `continue` when `entry.position <= position`, `break` when `entry.position != position + 1`, otherwise put the row, append to `log`, move `position` and count it.

`isAcknowledged`: write a local `fun has(f: Node) = (confirmed[f.name] ?: 0) >= entry.position`, then a `when (mode)`. For semi-sync the order of checks matters: off, then any follower has it, then the timeout (which sets `semiSyncOn = false` and returns true).

`failover`: `followers.filter { it.alive }.maxByOrNull { it.position }` keeps the first of equals. Set `nextId` from `rows.keys.maxOrNull()`, compute `acknowledged.filter { it.entry.position > chosen.position }` before calling `promote`, and return both.
If the property test fails, jqwik prints the smallest delays and crash time that break it. Re-create that case in a plain test and print `cluster.acknowledged` and each follower's position.

drill.title: The acknowledgement rule, from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write `isAcknowledged(entry, waitedMs)` for the three modes: asynchronous, synchronous to N followers, and MySQL-style semi-synchronous with a timeout that switches the leader to asynchronous. `confirmed[name]` is each follower's highest confirmed position.

recap: A replica is a full copy that keeps up with every change. Copies give availability, durability, nearby reads and read throughput; the difficulty is entirely in the changes.
Single-leader replication: one leader orders every write into a log with positions, and each follower applies the log in order. A follower's position says how up to date it is.

Asynchronous replication says OK before any follower has the write, so a failover can lose acknowledged writes. Fully synchronous replication lets one slow follower stop every write. Semi-synchronous waits for one follower; MySQL's falls back to asynchronous after a 10-second timeout without telling anyone.

A new follower is a consistent snapshot plus every log entry after the snapshot's exact position. A returning follower catches up from its position if the leader still has the log; otherwise it needs a new snapshot.

Failover is notice (a timeout), choose (the highest position), redirect. It can lose acknowledged writes, reuse ids that other systems still hold, and create split brain unless the old leader is fenced. GitHub's 2018 outage turned a 43-second partition into 24 hours and 11 minutes.

quiz.q: A MySQL 8.4 source runs semi-synchronous replication with its defaults and one replica. The replica's disk becomes very slow for two minutes. What do the applications see, and what is the risk?
options: Every commit fails with a timeout error for two minutes
Every commit takes about 10 seconds for two minutes
One commit takes about 10 seconds, then commits are fast again because the source has quietly become asynchronous; a failover in that window can lose acknowledged transactions
Nothing changes, because the replica acknowledges before writing to disk
quiz.why: On a timeout without an acknowledgement the source reverts to asynchronous replication and returns to semi-sync only when a replica catches up. Applications see one slow commit and no error. The replica acknowledges after the events are flushed to its relay log, so a slow disk does delay the ack. Only `Rpl_semi_sync_source_status` going to 0 tells you the guarantee is gone.

quiz.q: The leader dies. Follower A has applied up to position 9,812 and follower B up to 9,790. Replication was asynchronous. Which do you promote, and what have you lost?
options: A; every acknowledged write after 9,812, which was only on the dead leader
B, because it is less likely to have half-applied entries
Either; both will fetch the missing entries from the dead leader's disk
A; nothing, because B gives A entries 9,791 to 9,812
quiz.why: The most up-to-date follower loses the least, so promote A. Whatever the old leader acknowledged after 9,812 never reached any follower, so it is lost (until someone digs it out of the old leader's disk by hand). B is behind A, so it has nothing A lacks; it catches up from A. A dead leader can't send anything.

quiz.q: You add a follower from last night's snapshot, which was taken at position 51,000. You start it with "replay everything after 48,000" by mistake. Entries 48,001 to 51,000 include `UPDATE accounts SET fee = fee + 30 WHERE ...`. What happens if the log ships statements?
options: Nothing: the follower notices it already has those entries and skips them
The follower charges those fees a second time, and its data differs from the leader's from then on
The follower refuses to start because the positions don't match
Only the inserts are applied twice; updates are always safe
quiz.why: The snapshot already contains the effect of entries up to 51,000. Replaying from 48,000 applies 3,000 entries a second time, and a relative update like `fee = fee + 30` adds the fee again. The follower can only skip what it knows it has, and it was told the wrong position. Lesson 2 shows how row-based logs that carry the resulting values make a repeat harmless.

quiz.q: After an asynchronous failover, a service that caches `payment_id -> merchant` in Redis starts showing some merchants other merchants' payments. What is the most likely cause?
options: Redis evicted the keys under memory pressure
The new leader is serving reads from a stale snapshot
The new leader handed out ids of payments that were lost in the failover, and Redis still maps those ids to the old payments
Split brain: both leaders are writing to Redis
quiz.why: The promoted follower's auto-increment counter starts after the highest id it holds. The lost payments had ids above that, and the cache still has them, so new payments with the same ids look like the old ones. This is GitHub's 2012 incident. Eviction would cause misses, not wrong answers, and split brain needs the old leader to be alive and writing.

quiz.q: A Redis replica reconnects after 20 seconds away with `PSYNC <replid> <offset>`. When does it get a partial resync instead of a full one?
options: Always, as long as the master has the same replication id
When the master's replication backlog still holds everything after the replica's offset
Only if the replica was away for less than `repl-timeout`
When the replica has persistence (RDB or AOF) turned on
quiz.why: A partial resync sends only the stream after the replica's offset, and the master can do that only if its backlog, a fixed-size buffer, still covers the gap. If the replica fell further behind than the backlog holds, the master sends a full snapshot. It is this lesson's catch-up rule: a position is useful only while the leader still has the log after it.

flashcards.front: What does a follower's log position tell you?
flashcards.back: How far it has applied the leader's log: everything up to that position is in its data. Comparing positions tells you which copy is most up to date and how far behind each one is.

flashcards.front: Asynchronous replication: when does the client hear OK, and what can a failover lose?
flashcards.back: As soon as the leader's own disk has the write. A failover loses every acknowledged write the promoted follower had not yet received.

flashcards.front: Why not wait for every follower?
flashcards.back: Then each commit waits for the slowest follower, and one follower that is paused or down stops all writes.

flashcards.front: What does MySQL semi-sync do when no replica acknowledges within rpl_semi_sync_source_timeout (10 s)?
flashcards.back: The source reverts to asynchronous replication without any error to clients, and returns to semi-sync when a replica catches up. Watch Rpl_semi_sync_source_status.

flashcards.front: How does a new follower get started without stopping the leader?
flashcards.back: From a consistent snapshot plus the exact log position it reflects; it then applies every entry after that position and keeps streaming.

flashcards.front: What are the three steps of a failover?
flashcards.back: Notice the leader is gone (a timeout), choose the most up-to-date follower, redirect writes to it (and make the old leader rejoin as a follower).

flashcards.front: What is split brain, and what prevents it?
flashcards.back: Two nodes both accepting writes as leader, so their data diverges. Fencing prevents it: make sure the old leader can't write before or as the new one starts.

terms.plain: A copy of the whole database on another machine that keeps up with every change.
The one node that accepts writes and decides their order (primary, source).
A node that applies the leader's log in order and can serve reads (standby, replica, secondary).
The leader says OK before any follower has the write.
The leader waits for one follower (or some), not all; MySQL's version falls back to asynchronous after a timeout.
Making a follower the new leader after the leader fails, and pointing writes at it.
Two nodes that both act as leader and accept writes.
Stopping an old leader from writing, so that only the new one can.

explain_back.prompt: A product manager asks why "we have three copies of the database" doesn't mean a payment can never be lost or the service never goes down. Explain it in plain words.
explain_back.answer: Only one of the three copies, the leader, takes writes; it puts them in order and the other two copy that order. By default the leader tells the payment service OK as soon as it has saved the payment itself, and the copies receive it a few milliseconds later. If the leader's machine dies inside those milliseconds, the payment is on no surviving machine, although we told the customer it went through. We can make the leader wait until one copy confirms, which costs a little time on every payment and closes that gap, but then a stuck copy slows or stops payments, and some databases quietly stop waiting after a timeout. When the leader dies, nothing accepts payments until a copy is promoted, and we only promote after a timeout, so there are seconds of failed payments. Promotion itself has traps: a copy that is behind can reuse payment numbers, and if the old leader comes back and keeps accepting writes we have two diverging ledgers. So three copies make losing everything very unlikely, but losing the last few payments and a short outage are still possible unless we pay for synchronous copies and careful failover.

deeper.body:
Databases on object storage change the picture. A growing set of systems (WarpStream and Bufstream for Kafka-compatible logs, SlateDB, Turbopuffer) keep their log and data in S3-style object storage and use conditional writes, a compare-and-set on an object, to decide which node is the leader. Nothing is replicated between nodes' disks at all: the object store's own replication is the durability, and the conditional write is the fencing. Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 6 has a sidebar on this design.

Raft-based databases (CockroachDB, TiDB, etcd, YugabyteDB) are single-leader too, per range of keys, but they wait for a majority on every write and elect leaders by majority vote. That closes both of this lesson's failover holes at once: an acknowledged write is on a majority, and any new leader must win a majority, which must include a node that has the write. The Consistency and consensus track builds this from the ground up.

The words "synchronous" and "semi-synchronous" mean different things in different manuals. MySQL's semisynchronous replication waits for a replica to receive and flush the events; PostgreSQL's `synchronous_commit = remote_write` waits for less, and `remote_apply` for more. Before you trust a setting, find out exactly which of the five points in this lesson's figure it waits for, and what it does when no follower answers.

If you run MongoDB: `w: 1` writes are acknowledged by the primary alone, and when a primary is deposed before replicating them, they are rolled back and written to a rollback directory on disk for someone to inspect. The default write concern since MongoDB 5.0 is `w: "majority"`, which makes that much rarer.
